title: Impossible Stones
yt_title: Impossible Stones: How Do You Move 1,000 Tonnes?
hook: How do you move a 1,000-tonne stone?

lines: [d:intrigue][sfx:boom][act:hushed wonder, drawing them in]In a quarry in Lebanon lies a single block of stone as heavy as a thousand ^cars. [p:0.93][act:the number lands, slow][tune:fall]About sixteen hundred and fifty ^*tonnes*.

[d:tension][act:quickening, a teaser][tune:level]Nearby, three of its cousins sit high in a temple wall, each about nineteen metres ^long. [act:same pace, intrigued][tune:level]In Bolivia, hard grey blocks with razor-sharp inside ^corners. [act:same pace, a raised eyebrow][tune:fall]In Peru, walls so tight that a knife blade won't go ^in.

[d:wonder][act:the child's question, wide-eyed][tune:rise]So how could anyone move a ^thousand-tonne stone? [act:reporting the other answer, even][tune:fall]On television, the answer is often: they ^couldn't, not without a lost ^technology.

lines: [d:calm][act:plain, orienting]This is ^Baalbek, in Lebanon's Beqaa ^valley. [act:easy storytelling]About two thousand years ago it was a Roman colony, ^Heliopolis, crowned by a vast temple to ^Jupiter. [p:0.93][act:giving the size, a touch of awe]Its platform holds the ^trilithon: three limestone blocks, each about nineteen metres long, almost two buses end to ^end.

[d:build][p:0.93][act:careful, an honest wrinkle]Each weighs about eight hundred tonnes, by the classic ^estimate@noun. [act:same, precise]The German team working there reckons nearer a ^*thousand*. [act:wonder creeping in]And in the quarry, less than a kilometre away, lie three even bigger ^blocks: [act:counting them off][tune:level]about a thousand tonnes, about twelve hundred, [act:the last one, slow][tune:fall]and the one found in {2014|twenty fourteen}, about sixteen hundred and ^fifty.

shots.say: About two thousand years ago it was a ... by a vast temple to Jupiter.
shots.draw: A 16:9 map of Lebanon and its neighbours, View(34.6, 37.6, 32.9, 35.2): the Mediterranean, Beirut, Damascus; a gold pin 'Baalbek', the Beqaa valley labelled in italic, a 50 km scale bar. At 'Heliopolis' a small temple glyph (columns and pediment) draws itself above the pin with a glow; 'Roman Heliopolis' under it.
shots.reuse: baalbek_m() shot 1 (map + temple glyph), redrawn wide

shots.say: Its platform holds the trilithon: three limestone blocks, ... almost two buses end to end.
shots.draw: The western wall of the temple platform in elevation, to one scale (about 38 units a metre): the course of six blocks below, the trilithon above; the three giants outline in gold one by one; a dimension '19 m' draws along the middle one; two 12 m buses rise under it at 'two buses'; a 1.7 m person at the foot.
shots.reuse: baalbek_m() shot 0 (giants, buses), redrawn as an elevation

shots.say: Each weighs about eight hundred tonnes, by the ... working there reckons nearer a thousand.

shots.say: And in the quarry, less than a kilometre ... fourteen, about sixteen hundred and fifty.
shots.draw: The quarry as an iso model: three blocks lying in it (the tilted Stone of the Pregnant Woman, the 2014 block, the block found in the 1990s), each outlining in gold as its weight is said: '1,000 t', '1,240 t', '1,650 t'; a person for scale.

lines: [d:build][act:fair-minded, taking it seriously][tune:rise]The writer Graham ^Hancock asks a fair question: are these giant lower courses ^older than the Roman temple on ^top? [act:his reasons, even]Nothing else the Romans built uses blocks this ^big, [act:a telling detail, pointed][tune:fall]and no Roman writer ever boasts about moving ^them.

shots.say: The writer Graham Hancock asks a fair question: ... writer ever boasts about moving them.
shots.draw: The wall elevation again, now with the Roman temple on top (columns and roof drawn in bone); the giant courses get a lilac dotted outline and 'older?'. At 'Nothing else the Romans built' a row of ordinary Roman blocks pops beside them ('usual'); at 'no Roman writer' a scroll with blank lines and 'no boast'.

lines: [d:build][p:0.93][act:the method, curious][tune:rise]So how do you date a ^wall? [act:plain, a small smile][tune:fall]Not by its ^stone: the limestone is millions of years ^old. [act:a quick aside, light]One geologist dated ancient cart ruts in Turkey that way, and got a date before ^humans. [p:0.93][act:the analogy, clear][tune:fall]That's like dating a road by the age of the hill it ^climbs.

[d:build][act:explaining, a picture]You date what the builders left ^behind. [act:confident, matter of fact]German archaeologists have studied Baalbek on and off since {1898|eighteen ninety-eight}. [act:uncovering it, slower][tune:level]Inside the Roman platform sits an ^older, smaller ^one, [act:gently deflating, dry][tune:fall]built of ordinary ^blocks. [act:explaining, clear and steady]The giant platform wraps around it, like a new coat over an old ^one: so the giants came ^later.

shots.say: So how do you date a wall? Not ... limestone is millions of years old.
shots.draw: A limestone block in section: fine sea layers inside it; a clock tag 'rock: millions of years' on the layers; a chisel mark on its face with a lilac tag 'cut: when?'.

shots.say: One geologist dated ancient cart ruts in Turkey ... age of the hill it climbs.
shots.draw: Left: two cart ruts cut in a slab of bare rock, running away in perspective, a cart wheel in one ('cart ruts'); a lilac tag 'before humans?' struck through in red. Right, as the analogy comes: a big old hill, and a new road winding up it with a small car; tags 'hill: very old' and 'road: new'.
shots.reuse: cart-ruts cart_ruts_m() rockage (the rock's age is not the groove's)

shots.say: You date what the builders left behind. German ... on and off since eighteen ninety-eight.
shots.draw: An excavation trench in section at dusk: two archaeologists, a trowel, a sieve, a lamp; six columns of the temple on the skyline; a thin timeline at the top from 1898 to today, gold where the German work ran (1898 to 1905, and from 1997): 'German digs, on and off'.

shots.say: Inside the Roman platform sits an older, smaller ... one: so the giants came later.
shots.draw: The platform cut open (section): inside, a smaller, older terrace of ordinary blocks builds course by course ('older terrace', 1); then the giant blocks wrap around it on both sides ('2'), a gold arrow 'later'.

lines: [d:reveal][act:the clincher, measured]In the quarry, the team found a few scraps of pottery that can be ^dated: [act:the key point][tune:fall]early Roman ^times. [act:an engineer's eye, admiring]The block found in {2014|twenty fourteen} is as long as the trilithon's, cut for a third course that was never ^laid. [p:0.93][act:plain, a little rueful]The platform was planned three or four courses ^high. [act:the landing, quiet][tune:fall]Only two were ^finished.

[d:aside][act:fair, the silence][tune:rise]And the Roman ^silence? [act:plainly][tune:fall]Most of their building records@noun are simply ^lost. [act:plain, a little rueful]An empty shelf can't tell you what was never ^written.

[d:calm][act:curious, a side question][tune:rise]And why leave the biggest blocks ^behind? [p:0.93][act:explaining, careful]The Stone of the Pregnant Woman has hollows and cracks along one ^edge. [act:a practical shrug][tune:fall]It might have broken on the ^road.

shots.say: In the quarry, the team found a few ... can be dated: early Roman times.
shots.draw: The quarry floor at dusk: a heap of stone chips; three potsherds glow one after another, a tag 'early Roman' pops.

shots.say: The block found in twenty fourteen is as ... courses high. Only two were finished.
shots.draw: The podium in elevation: course 1 (the six-block course) and course 2 (the trilithon) solid; course 3 drawn dashed with the 2014 block's outline ghosted into it ('never laid'); course 4 dashed with '?'. Labels 'planned: 3 or 4 courses', then 'built: 2'.

shots.say: And the Roman silence? Most of their building ... tell you what was never written.
shots.draw: A shelf of scrolls and tablets: two solid, the rest dotted outlines that fade in ('lost').

shots.say: And why leave the biggest blocks behind? The ... might have broken on the road.
shots.draw: The Stone of the Pregnant Woman lying tilted in the quarry (elevation): cracks draw along one edge and dark hollows (karst) open in it; a dashed road leads off towards the temple with a small break sign on it.

lines: [d:calm][p:0.93][act:the child's question, inviting][tune:rise]So, how ^do you move a thousand-tonne stone? [act:explaining, simple]The enemy isn't really the ^weight. [act:the twist][tune:fall]It's ^friction: stone grinding against ^ground. [p:0.93][act:an everyday picture, light]Think of shoving a fridge across a carpet, then rolling it on a ^trolley. [act:the answer, light][tune:fall]Put a stone on a sledge, on a smooth track, and you're halfway ^there.

shots.say: The enemy isn't really the weight. It's friction: stone grinding against ground.
shots.draw: A stone block on bare ground pushed by a line of tiny people; at the contact, short red friction marks flicker; label 'friction'.

shots.say: Think of shoving a fridge across a carpet, then rolling it on a trolley.
shots.draw: Left: a person shoving a fridge across a carpet, the carpet rucking up, red marks. Right: the same fridge on a trolley rolling, a light arrow.

shots.say: Put a stone on a sledge, on a smooth track, and you're halfway there.
shots.draw: The block on a timber sledge running on a track of cross-timbers; a long arrow shows it gliding; label 'sledge + track'.

lines: [d:build][act:storytelling, onward]About three thousand nine hundred years ago, an Egyptian governor named ^Djehutihotep had a scene painted in his ^tomb. [p:0.93][act:describing it, vivid]A colossal statue of about sixty tonnes, on a sledge, hauled by a hundred and seventy-two ^men. [act:the clue, hushed][tune:fall]And at the front, one man pours ^water onto the sand. [act:fair, the other reading][tune:level]Some Egyptologists read@present that as a ^ritual. [act:a smile][tune:rise]Engineers asked: does@verb it ^help?

[d:reveal][act:the experiment, delighted]In {2014|twenty fourteen}, a team of physicists in Amsterdam tested it, with a model sledge in a tray of ^sand. [p:0.9][act:the result, precise]With just the right amount of water, the sand stiffens, and the pull you need drops by about ^*half*. [act:an everyday picture, light][tune:fall]Like walking on wet sand at the beach, instead of ^dry.

[d:build][act:widening out, curious]Other experiments keep finding cheap ^tricks. [p:0.93][act:vivid, delighted]In Hawaii, eighteen people with three ropes rocked a replica Easter Island statue of more than four tonnes from side to side, [act:the payoff, light][tune:fall]and walked it a hundred metres in forty minutes@time.

shots.say: About three thousand nine hundred years ago, an ... ritual. Engineers asked: does it help?
shots.draw: The tomb painting of Djehutihotep, redrawn schematically in ochre and black on a plaster panel: a seated colossal statue on a sledge ('60 t'); four rows of 43 pullers (172 small figures) pop in along the ropes ('172 men'); a man at the front pours water from a jar, blue drops ('water'). At 'ritual' a lilac tag 'ritual?' beside the pourer; at 'does it help?' a gold '?' over the wet sand.

shots.say: In twenty fourteen, a team of physicists in ... at the beach, instead of dry.
shots.draw: A lab tray of sand with a model sledge: on dry sand a berm piles up in front and a long force arrow; on wet sand no berm and an arrow half as long; label 'about half'. Then, as the beach is named: two footprints, deep in dry sand, shallow on wet.

shots.say: Other experiments keep finding cheap tricks. In Hawaii, ... a hundred metres in forty minutes.
shots.draw: Daylight: a replica Easter Island statue seen from the front ('4.35 t replica'); two faint ghosts show it rocked onto one corner, then the other; three ropes from its head to three teams of six ('18 people'); a dashed 100 m path and an arrow: '100 m in 40 min'.

lines: [d:build][act:explaining, a picture]Romans had better ^kit. [p:0.93][act:explaining, clear]A capstan is an upright wooden drum: people push its bars, walk in a circle, and the rope winds@coil ^in. [act:brisk, glad to explain]In {1977|nineteen seventy-seven}, the architect Jean-Pierre ^Adam did the sums for Baalbek. [sfx:hit][act:counting them off, deliberate][tune:level]^Six capstans, with pulleys. [act:adding up, same pace][tune:level]A hundred and forty-four ^people. [act:the payoff, firm][tune:fall]One eight-hundred-tonne ^block.

shots.say: Romans had better kit. A capstan is an ... circle, and the rope winds in.
shots.draw: A capstan: an upright wooden drum with four bars; four people push the bars and walk in a circle (a circular arrow); the rope winds onto the drum and runs off to a block.

shots.say: In nineteen seventy-seven, the architect Jean-Pierre Adam did ... and forty-four people. One eight-hundred-tonne block.
shots.draw: Jean-Pierre Adam's layout: the 800-tonne block on a timber track; ahead of it six capstans in a row, each ringed by 24 small figures (144 in all); ropes run back to the block; counters '6 capstans', '144 people', '800 t'.

lines: [d:reveal][act:a raised eyebrow][tune:rise]Sums on ^paper? [act:the reveal, delighted]Then here's the real ^thing. [p:0.93][act:storytelling, vivid]In {1770|seventeen seventy}, in Russia, about four hundred people hauled a granite boulder of more than a thousand tonnes some six kilometres over ^land, [act:the method, clear]on a sledge rolling over bronze ^balls, pulled by ^capstans. [act:a quiet image, warm]It still carries a bronze horseman in Saint ^Petersburg. [act:the comparison, pointed][tune:fall]When it moved, it outweighed any block in Baalbek's ^wall. [act:the kicker, dry][tune:fall]No lost technology. [act:same rhythm][tune:fall]Just ^people, rope and ^patience.

shots.say: Sums on paper? Then here's the real thing. ... over bronze balls, pulled by capstans.
shots.draw: A snowy plain at dusk, '1770': the Thunder Stone, a huge granite boulder, rides a timber sledge on a track; two capstans ahead and a crowd of tiny figures ('about 400 people'); a dashed route line '6 km over land'. At 'bronze balls' a round magnifier opens over the track: the sledge beam above, the track below, bronze balls between them.

shots.say: It still carries a bronze horseman in Saint ... technology. Just people, rope and patience.
shots.draw: The boulder today as a pedestal, a rearing horse and rider in bronze-green silhouette on top ('Saint Petersburg'); then a balance: the boulder ('over 1,000 t') outweighs a Baalbek giant ('800 to 1,000 t'). At 'No lost technology' that line appears in gold, and three icons light up as named: a person ('people'), a coil ('rope'), a clock ('patience').

lines: [d:tension][act:fair, the open part][tune:level]What we don't know is the exact recipe at ^Baalbek: [act:honest, plain]how the giants were raised onto the course below, and nudged into ^place. [act:a small shrug][tune:fall]Ramps and levers, most likely, but nobody left the ^instructions.

shots.say: What we don't know is the exact recipe ... likely, but nobody left the instructions.
shots.draw: The trilithon wall in elevation: one giant hovers in a dashed outline above its course with a lilac '?'; a dashed earth ramp draws up to the course; a lever pokes under the block; a blank sheet labelled 'instructions?'.

lines: [d:calm][act:plain storytelling, warm]High in the Andes of Bolivia, at three thousand eight hundred and fifty metres, lies Puma ^Punku, a stone platform in the ancient city of ^Tiwanaku. [act:the marvel, unhurried]Its hard grey andesite blocks are cut into H-shapes with crisp inside ^corners, [act:a picture][tune:fall]like pieces of a ^kit. [act:a little sad, plain]Today they lie broken and scattered, as if a giant toy box had been tipped ^out.

[d:build][act:matter of fact, steady]The andesite came from about ninety kilometres away, across or around Lake ^Titicaca. [act:a quick contrast, lighter]The red sandstone came from just ^ten. [p:0.9][act:weighing it out, impressed]Its biggest slab weighs about a hundred and thirty-one ^tonnes.

shots.say: Its hard grey andesite blocks are cut into ... corners, like pieces of a kit.
shots.draw: Four andesite H-blocks (iso, turning): the inside corners glow and an amber template outline traces over each in turn.

shots.say: Today they lie broken and scattered, as if a giant toy box had been tipped out.
shots.draw: Seen from above, a field of broken, tilted blocks scattered across the platform; a few H-shapes among them.

shots.say: The andesite came from about ninety kilometres away, ... red sandstone came from just ten.
shots.draw: A map of Lake Titicaca (View(-70.4, -67.6, -17.6, -15.0)): gold pin 'Tiwanaku', 'Copacabana', 'La Paz'; a dashed gold route '90 km' draws across the lake. At 'red sandstone', a small red ring '10 km' around Tiwanaku.

shots.say: Its biggest slab weighs about a hundred and thirty-one tonnes.
shots.draw: The red sandstone slab as an iso model, 7.8 x 5.2 x 1.1 m, to scale with a 1.7 m person; dimension lines '7.8 m' and '5.2 m'; label '131 t'.

lines: [d:build][act:storytelling, intrigued]The explorer Arthur ^Posnansky measured where Tiwanaku's temple walls point, against the sky. [p:0.93][act:explaining, a simple picture]Over thousands of years the sky slowly ^drifts, so a wall aimed at a sunrise long ago no longer lines up ^today. [act:the big claim, let it land][tune:fall]From the mismatch, he dated the city to about fifteen thousand ^BCE. [act:brisk, matter of fact]In the {1990s|nineteen nineties}, Graham Hancock revived that ^date. [act:a light, dry report][tune:fall]And on television, the blocks are called ^machined: too precise for hand ^tools.

shots.say: The explorer Arthur Posnansky measured where Tiwanaku's temple ... ago no longer lines up today.
shots.draw: Dawn horizon: a wall aimed at the horizon (a gold sight line); a lilac sun 'long ago' sits on the line; an arrow 'the sky drifts'; a gold sun 'today' rises beside it; the angle between them draws as 'mismatch'.

shots.say: From the mismatch, he dated the city to ... nineties, Graham Hancock revived that date.
shots.draw: A timeline from 16,000 BCE to today: a lilac dotted dot '15,000 BCE?' with 'Posnansky'; at 'Graham Hancock', a small book pops with '1990s'.

shots.say: And on television, the blocks are called machined: too precise for hand tools.
shots.draw: The TV set again: on its screen an H-block with a lilac gear turning; 'machined?' in lilac.

lines: [d:build][act:the turn, crisp][tune:fall]Then came ^radiocarbon. [p:0.93][act:explaining, clear]Living things take in a trace of radioactive carbon, which fades after death at a steady pace, like a candle burning ^down. [act:precise, reading the lab result]Organic material from the lowest fill of the platform: about AD {536|five thirty-six} to {600|six hundred}. [act:explaining, fair, not gloating]Posnansky's method had a weak ^spot: misjudge what a wall was aimed at by a sliver of a degree, and the date swings by ^thousands of years.

shots.say: Then came radiocarbon. Living things take in a ... pace, like a candle burning down.
shots.draw: A plant takes in carbon (green dots); then a candle beside it burns down, a bar 'what's left' measuring it.

shots.say: Organic material from the lowest fill of the platform: about AD five thirty-six to six hundred.
shots.draw: The platform in section: andesite and sandstone courses on top, the lowest fill below; green specks glow in it; 'lowest fill', then 'AD 536 to 600' (serif, gold). The timeline returns below with a short gold band at the far right and the 15,000 BCE dot struck out.

shots.say: Posnansky's method had a weak spot: misjudge what ... date swings by thousands of years.
shots.draw: Two lines leave one point a sliver of a degree apart; far away they are far apart; at the end the gap reads 'thousands of years' (red double arrow).

lines: [d:reveal][act:leaning in, a new clue]And the ^metal. [act:vivid, building]Some blocks were locked together with I-shaped ^cramps, poured molten into sockets carved across the ^joint. [act:the clincher, quiet and sure]The alloy, copper, arsenic and ^nickel, belongs to Tiwanaku's own ^era.

[d:build][act:admiring, even]Architects who measured the blocks found repeated designs, as if cut from ^patterns, like a dressmaker's ^template. [act:fair, a nuance][tune:fall]But no two are quite the same size, so not a true ^kit. [p:0.93][act:honest, curious][tune:rise]And the tools that cut those sharp inside ^corners? [act:a small shrug][tune:fall]Still ^unknown.

shots.say: And the metal. Some blocks were locked together ... nickel, belongs to Tiwanaku's own era.
shots.draw: Two andesite blocks meet at a joint; an I-shaped socket outlines across it; a crucible tips and orange molten bronze fills the socket; then three element dots: copper, arsenic, nickel; 'Tiwanaku's own era'.

shots.say: Architects who measured the blocks found repeated designs, ... size, so not a true kit.
shots.draw: Three H-block profiles side by side; a dashed amber template slides over each; small mismatches glow where the template and the stone differ ('not identical').

shots.say: And the tools that cut those sharp inside corners? Still unknown.
shots.draw: A close-up of a sharp inside corner, lit; a lilac question mark; a faint hammerstone outline and a struck-through gear; label 'tools: unknown'.

lines: [d:calm][act:plain, placing it]Now, Peru, above ^Cusco, the old Inca ^capital. [act:painting the picture]Three terraced walls ^zigzag across a hill here for about four hundred metres: ^Sacsayhuamán. [act:admiring, slower]Some stones weigh well over a hundred ^tonnes, cut into many-sided shapes, [act:the marvel][tune:fall]and fitted so tightly, without mortar, that a knife blade won't slide ^between them.

shots.say: Three terraced walls zigzag across a hill here for about four hundred metres: Sacsayhuamán.
shots.draw: Sacsayhuamán's three zigzag terraces as an iso model on the green hill; the zigzags trace in gold one after another; a dimension 'about 400 m' along the top; the name in gold.

shots.say: Some stones weigh well over a hundred tonnes, ... knife blade won't slide between them.
shots.draw: The polygonal wall (the hook's jigsaw panel, closer): one giant outlined in gold '100+ t'; its many corners dot in turn; the knife at a joint; 'no mortar'.

lines: [d:build][act:fair-minded, presenting the case]Some writers say these giants are ^older, and the Incas only built on ^top. [act:pointing, inviting a look][tune:level]Huge, perfect@adj blocks at the ^bottom; [act:the contrast][tune:fall]smaller, rougher stones ^above. [act:their logic, fair][tune:rise]Two styles, two ^builders?

shots.say: Some writers say these giants are older, and ... stones above. Two styles, two builders?
shots.draw: The wall in elevation: giant polygonal stones at the bottom ('1', 'huge, perfect'), two rows of small rough stones above ('2', 'smaller, rougher'); a lilac dotted box round the giants, 'older?'; at the end 'two builders?'.

lines: [d:build][act:historical, steady]In {1536|fifteen thirty-six}, Spanish soldiers fought the Incas over these very ^walls. [act:the key point, calm]Chroniclers writing within a generation describe an ^Inca work. [act:quoting the source, impressed]One of them, Pedro Cieza de ^León, reports twenty thousand workers, taking ^turns. [act:counting them off][tune:level]Four thousand ^quarrying. [act:finishing the count][tune:fall]Six thousand hauling with ^ropes. [act:simple, a little sad][tune:rise]And the rougher upper ^walls? [act:the explanation, clear][tune:fall]Mostly ^gone: after the siege, stone that could be moved was carted down to build colonial ^Cusco. [act:the payoff, plain][tune:fall]What's left at the bottom are the giants: too big to ^shift.

shots.say: In fifteen thirty-six, Spanish soldiers fought the Incas ... a generation describe an Inca work.
shots.draw: A timeline 1500 to 1580: crossed swords at 1536 ('the siege'); an arc 'a generation' to a chronicle book at about 1553 ('an Inca work').

shots.say: One of them, Pedro Cieza de León, reports ... quarrying. Six thousand hauling with ropes.
shots.draw: 200 small figures, each 100 workers ('each figure: 100 workers'); 40 turn amber ('4,000 quarrying'), 60 turn blue ('6,000 hauling').

shots.say: And the rougher upper walls? Mostly gone: after ... the giants: too big to shift.
shots.draw: The hill in elevation: the upper courses drawn as dotted ghosts ('gone'); arrows carry small stones down to the houses and tower of colonial Cusco; the giants at the bottom glow ('too big to shift').

lines: [d:reveal][act:the experiment, curious][tune:rise]And the perfect@adj ^fit? [act:storytelling, onward]In the {1980s|nineteen eighties}, the architect Jean-Pierre ^Protzen picked up hammerstones like those the Incas left in their ^quarries. [p:0.93][act:precise, impressed]With one of about four kilos, he dressed a face of a small block in twenty minutes@time. [act:practical, a craftsman's rhythm]To fit two stones: lower one onto the other, see where it ^touches, pound those spots down, ^repeat. [act:warm, the payoff][tune:fall]His joints came close@adj to the Incas' ^own.

[d:build][act:the moving part, plain]At the Inca quarry for ^Ollantaytambo, he mapped their ramps, up to eight metres wide, [act:a quiet detail][tune:fall]with about eighty blocks abandoned along the ^way.

shots.say: And the perfect fit? In the nineteen eighties, ... a small block in twenty minutes.

lines: [d:verdict][p:0.93][act:fair, a concession]People did live@verb on that hill before the ^Incas, from about {900|nine hundred} CE. [act:precise, the crux][tune:fall]But no older wall has been ^dated.

lines: [d:verdict][act:stepping back, calm]So, the ^ledger. [act:clear, counting them off][tune:level]A lost high technology, needed to move these stones: *ruled ^out*. [act:same steady pace][tune:level]Baalbek's giants older than Rome: *awaiting ^evidence*. [act:same pace][tune:level]Exactly how the trilithon was raised: an *open ^question*.

[act:same pace][tune:level]Puma Punku in fifteen thousand BCE: *ruled ^out*. [act:same pace][tune:level]How its sharp corners were cut: *open ^question*. [act:same pace][tune:level]Older builders under Sacsayhuamán: *awaiting ^evidence*. [act:closing the column][tune:fall]Inca hammerstones behind that fit: *strong ^evidence*.

[d:calm][p:0.95][act:the whole picture, warm]Taken together, a *mixed ^record@noun*. [act:clear, fair]Wherever we can check, the evidence points to people archaeology already knows: the ^Romans, the builders of ^Tiwanaku, the ^Incas. [act:tender, a little wonder][tune:fall]What's lost isn't a ^machine. [act:the last word of it][tune:fall]It's the know-how of people who rarely wrote it ^down. [act:warm, sincere]That makes the stones more ^impressive, not less: they're monuments to ^people.

lines: [d:tension][act:practical, counting them off][tune:rise]What would change our ^minds? [act:same beat][tune:level]At Baalbek, a sealed layer under the trilithon: Roman pottery beneath it would close@verb the file, and only older finds would reopen ^it. [act:same beat][tune:level]At Sacsayhuamán, one charcoal date from the fill behind the ^giants. [act:same beat][tune:level]At Puma Punku, a replica, cut with tools of the time, that matches those ^corners. [act:the last one, a smile][tune:fall]And for the lost technology, just one thing it left behind: a ^tool, a ^workshop, a ^drill bit.

description:
In a quarry in Lebanon lies a block of stone of about 1,650 tonnes, the largest known from the ancient world. In Bolivia, hard grey blocks with razor-sharp inside corners; in Peru, walls so tight a knife blade won't go in. On television they are often called impossible without a lost technology.

We weigh Baalbek, Puma Punku and Sacsayhuamán claim by claim, with each challenger at their strongest, and answer the child's question: how do you move a thousand-tonne stone? Sledges, wet sand, capstans, ramps and levers, a granite boulder hauled by hand in 1770, and the experiments that tested them. Verdict: Mixed record. Weigh it yourself.

facts_added.fact: The trilithon blocks are about 19.6 m long and 4.35 m high and, by the German Archaeological Institute's reckoning, weigh about 1,000 t each; the classic estimate (Adam 1977 and most guides) is about 800 t. Sources disagree, and the film says so.
facts_added.source: van Ess 2015, e-Forschungsberichte des DAI; Adam 1977, Syria 54

facts_added.fact: The podium of the Temple of Jupiter was planned with three or four courses (13.45 m high); only two were built. The block found in 2014 has the trilithon's length and was cut for the third course.
Few but well-datable pottery fragments from the quarry point to quarrying in the early Roman imperial period.

The 2014 block measures 19.6 x 6 x at least 5.5 m and weighs about 1,650 t; it lies beside and partly beneath the Hajjar al-Hibla (Stone of the Pregnant Woman); it is the largest stone block known from antiquity.
facts_added.source: DAI press release, December 2014 (HeritageDaily; DigVentures); van Ess 2015

facts_added.fact: The Hajjar al-Hibla (about 1,000 t) was left in the quarry because of poor stone quality along one edge (karst cavities and cracks) that could have broken it in transport; it was never cut free of the bedrock.
facts_added.source: DAI press release, December 2014; van Ess 2015

facts_added.fact: The Roman platform of the Temple of Jupiter was raised over an earlier, pre-Roman base (a podium, staircase and foundation walls) that was incorporated into the Roman master plan.
facts_added.source: Lohmann 2010, Bollettino di Archeologia On Line

facts_added.fact: Systematic German excavation at Baalbek began in 1898 after the visit of Kaiser Wilhelm II (Otto Puchstein's expedition worked until 1904); the DAI and Lebanon's Directorate General of Antiquities have run a joint programme since 1997.
facts_added.source: Wiegand (ed.) 1921-1925, Baalbek: Ergebnisse der Ausgrabungen und Untersuchungen in den Jahren 1898 bis 1905; DAI Baalbek project (joint programme with the DGA since 1997)

facts_added.fact: The tomb painting of the nomarch Djehutihotep at Deir el-Bersha (about 1880 BCE, Middle Kingdom) shows a colossal statue of about 6.8 m, estimated at about 58 to 60 t, on a sledge hauled by 172 men, with a man pouring liquid in front of the sledge. Newberry read the pouring as a ceremonial act; engineers read it as lubrication.
facts_added.source: Newberry 1895; Habachi 1984, as cited by Dziedzic (bibliotekanauki.pl article 1683708: about 60 t, 172 men); Nosonovsky (UWM essay: the ritual and lubrication readings)

facts_added.fact: With the right amount of water, desert sand becomes about twice as stiff and the force needed to pull a sledge over it falls by about half (laboratory experiment with a model sledge).
facts_added.source: Fall et al. 2014, Physical Review Letters 112: 175502, doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.112.175502

facts_added.fact: In 2012, at Kualoa Ranch in Hawaii, eighteen people with three hemp ropes rocked a 4.35-tonne concrete replica of an Easter Island moai from side to side and 'walked' it 100 m in about 40 minutes (under an hour).
facts_added.source: Lipo & Hunt 2025, Journal of Archaeological Science 183: 106383, doi:10.1016/j.jas.2025.106383; Lipo, Hunt & Rapu Haoa 2013, doi:10.1016/j.jas.2012.09.029; Live Science, 24 October 2012 (location and ropes)

facts_added.fact: The Thunder Stone, a granite boulder estimated at well over 1,000 t (estimates from about 1,250 to 1,500 t and more), was moved about 6 km overland in 1769-1770 by about 400 men, on a sledge running on bronze balls in grooved rails, pulled by capstans; it is the pedestal of the Bronze Horseman in Saint Petersburg.
facts_added.source: Carburi 1777; Guinness World Records (largest stone moved by manpower alone)

facts_added.fact: None of Pumapunku's roughly 150 surviving blocks is in its original position; the site was quarried and looted over centuries.
In Pumapunku's south canal the I-shaped cramps of copper-arsenic-nickel bronze were cast in place, poured into the sockets.

Pumapunku's blocks fall into about eleven repeated designs (some in left- and right-handed versions), but blocks of the same design vary in size and are not interchangeable like a true kit; the Tiahuanaco masons' tools remain essentially unknown, except perhaps hammerstones, and the sharp 90-degree interior angles were most likely not made with hammerstones.
facts_added.source: Protzen & Nair 1997, Journal of the Society of Architectural Historians 56(2): 146-167; Protzen & Nair 2013

facts_added.fact: Posnansky dated Tiwanaku's Kalasasaya to about 15,000 BCE from the change in the Earth's tilt (obliquity) against the wall's solstice alignment.
facts_added.source: Posnansky 1945, Tihuanacu: The Cradle of American Man

facts_added.fact: At an Inca quarry Protzen found 68 hammerstones of 2 to 8 kg; with a 4 kg hammerstone he dressed one face of a small andesite block in about 20 minutes, and fitted blocks by repeated trial lowering, marking and pounding (about 90 minutes for one fit), with results comparable to Inca masonry.
facts_added.source: Protzen 1985, Journal of the Society of Architectural Historians 44(2): 161-182; Protzen 1986, Scientific American 254(2)

facts_added.fact: At Kachiqhata, the quarry for Ollantaytambo, Inca access ramps are 4 to 8 m wide, and about 80 abandoned blocks lie along the routes.
facts_added.source: Protzen 1985, Journal of the Society of Architectural Historians 44(2): 161-182

facts_added.fact: The hill of Sacsayhuamán was occupied from about 900 CE (the Killke period) before the Incas built the terraces.
